cases.note: Shape written by the desktop writer (explanation gets a trailing newline).
Metadata is mandatory in LaTeX: a wrapper without it (the pre-2026-10-10 legacy form) is broken.
The retired 'Prepared in Codex conversation' fallback no longer supplies metadata.
The sentence does not complete created-only metadata either.
The sentence is ordinary explanation text; the conversation ID comes from the metadata only.
Fractional seconds are optional for readers.
\\ (line break) followed by % starts a comment, so the } after it is commented out.
\\\% is a line break followed by a literal percent sign, so the wrapper's } closes the argument.
Shape found in a real Library source (arguments on their own lines).
Spans are code points: each emoji counts 1 (2 UTF-16 units, 4 UTF-8 bytes).
A comment ends at LF; the CR before it belongs to the comment.
Readers return the explanation exactly as written; they do not undo the writer's TeX escaping.
The explanation must not be blank in either format (no real proposal has a blank one).
A wrapper inside a % comment is not live.
\\ is a line break; the following 'agentProposedEdit' is text.
Three backslashes: a line break followed by a live command.
A longer control word ([A-Za-z@]) is a different macro.
A command not followed by [ or { is a mention, not a wrapper and not an issue.
cases.source: The \agentProposedEdit macro wraps an edit; see \agentProposedEdit.

cases.note: An unbraced definition looks like a metadata argument; definition commands are recognised first.
Real shape: docs-reading_list/tex/source/main.tex lines 48-104 (\let at line 99).
DocCode is the user's fancyvrb Verbatim environment (1037 uses in real sources).
Inside verbatim, % and braces are literal.
An unclosed verbatim environment hides the rest of the file; that is not an issue.
A \begin{verbatim} inside a comment does not start verbatim.
LinkedDocCode sets commandchars=\\\{\}, so commands inside it run; it is not on the verbatim list.
Real shape from a Library source. Not part of the format.
A TeX wrapper in a .md file is text.
Real shape: ~/Thoughts/docs/library/README.md line 10.
A complete Markdown block in a .tex file is text.

Every wrapper whose id was read counts for duplicates, including broken ones.
Only the outermost wrapper is reported; wrappers inside it are not proposals.
\agentRemove inside an argument is ordinary text, so the wrapper is not nested.
A commented-out wrapper inside an argument is not a nested proposal.
Span: the command through its last complete argument.
A broken wrapper does not block decisions on its valid neighbours.
Everything after an unclosed argument belongs to it: one issue, later wrappers are not seen.

cases.note: No whitespace inside the metadata list.
Must be a real calendar date.
T and Z are uppercase.
At most nine fractional digits.
Both created and conversation_id are required.
Both created and conversation_id are required (writers always emit both).
Real legacy shape: created only.
Fixed order: created first.
Structured conversation IDs are lowercase.
An empty link is not an absent one.
Only the two link forms of 3.6.
Session IDs are letters and digits.
At most 64 characters after session_.
Codex thread UUIDs are lowercase.
Fixed order: the link comes last.
The link does not replace the conversation ID.
UTC with Z only; all 99 timestamps in real sources use Z.
The metadata is trimmed of ASCII whitespace as a whole, as without a link.
A wrapper without metadata still counts for duplicates: the valid one is duplicate_id, the bare one reports invalid_metadata (first in table order).
invalid_metadata precedes invalid_id; other proposals in the file stay decidable.
The retired \agentRemove wrapper is an unknown command: neither a proposal nor an issue.
Broken \agentRemove text produces no issue either.
